paper_title: PhysioWave-T: Token-Efficient Wavelet Foundation Models for Biosignals

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We present PhysioWave-T, a token-efficient wavelet foundation model family for EEG, ECG, and sEMG. Dynamic scale folding recombines J+1 wavelet subbands prior to tokenization, compressing sequence length from (J+1)CS to CS tokens for J levels, C channels, and S temporal patches. Route-specific front ends and learned channel-name embeddings allow one Transformer per modality to handle diverse montages and sampling rates, while unseen setups reuse the backbone via lightweight adapters. We pre-train a 30M-parameter EEG model on over 15M windows (19--128 channels), alongside ECG (30M) and sEMG (12M) encoders. Across four EEG routes, scale folding cuts Transformer latency by 4.0--7.2x and peak memory by 6.8--12.7x over scale expansion without accuracy loss. Our EEG encoder leads 8 of 9 metrics against BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, and EEGPT, and surpasses LUNA-L on wearable seizure detection with fewer parameters. Reliability-aware latent fusion (RALF) further integrates summary tokens from independently pre-trained encoders via sample-adaptive weights. On SeizeIT2, RALF raises event sensitivity at 11 false alarms/h from 61.4% to 74.4% and window AUPRC from 0.321 to 0.399 over the best unimodal baseline, outperforming weighted-logit and concatenation fusion across all variants. PhysioWave-T also achieves state-of-the-art sEMG accuracies and top macro-F1 on PTB-XL Super and Chapman-Shaoxing. Code and models: https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/PhysioWave.

sections.content: IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON PATTERN ANALYSIS AND MACHINE INTELLIGENCE 1 PhysioWave-T: Token-Efficient Wavelet Foundation Models for Biosignals Yanlong Chen, Simone Benatti, Luca Benini, Fellow, IEEE, Cuntai Guan, Fellow, IEEE, and Yawei Li AbstractWe present PhysioWave-T, token-efficient wavelet foundation-model family for electroencephalography (EEG), electrocardiography (ECG), and surface electromyography (sEMG). Dynamic scale folding recombines the J+1 wavelet subbands before tokenization, compressing the sequence from (J+1)CS to CS tokens for decomposition levels, channels, and temporal patches. Route-specific wavelet front ends and learned channel-name embeddings let one Transformer per modality accommodate diverse channel counts and sampling rates, while unseen configurations reuse the pre-trained backbone via lightweight front end. Together, these components scale PhysioWave to EEG: we pre-train 30M-parameter EEG foundation model on over 15M windows spanning 19 to 128 channels, alongside ECG (30M) and sEMG (12M) encoders. Across four EEG routes, folding cuts Transformer latency by 4.07.2 and peak memory by 6.812.7 over scale expansion without accuracy loss. The EEG encoder leads eight of nine metrics against BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, and EEGPT, and surpasses LUNA-L on wearable seizure detection with fewer parameters. Reliability-aware latent fusion (RALF) then integrates summary tokens from the independently pre-trained encoders using per-sample reliability weights. On SeizeIT2, fusion raises event sensitivity at 11 false alarms/h from 61.4 % to 74.4 % with RALF, while RALF boosts window-level AUPRC from 0.321 to 0.399 over the best unimodal model and outperforms weighted-logit and concatenation fusion in AUPRC across all six training variants. PhysioWave-T also sets new state-of-the-art sEMG accuracies and the highest macro-F1 on PTB-XL Super and ChapmanShaoxing, establishing an efficient, extensible foundation for biosignal representation learning. Code and models are available at https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/PhysioWave. Index TermsBiosignal foundation models, self-supervised learning, token efficiency, heterogeneous acquisition, multimodal fusion.

sections.content: of the human body across diverse temporal scales, yet their acquisition hardware and recording protocols are far from uniform. Across clinical and consumer settings, EEG spans two-channel wearables to 128-channel scalp arrays; ECG ranges from single-lead ambulatory patches to clinical twelve-lead systems; and sEMG is captured by wristbands, forearm arrays, and high-density grids, each governed by distinct sampling rate and sensor geometry. truly reusable representation must capture multiscale physiological structure while flexibly accommodating this hardware diversity, yet these two desiderata pull directly against each other. Wavelet decompositions are well suited to non-stationary biosignals, but exposing every scale to Transformer incurs steep quadratic cost: -level decomposition of channels and patches yields (J+1)CS tokens, causing channel density, window duration, and decomposition depth to lengthen the token sequence in Y. Mapping every recording onto single fixed input layout sidesteps this variability, but intermediate heuristics such as channel selection, padding, or resampling inevitably discard acquisition-specific information along the way. Our prior works, WaveFormer [1] and PhysioWave [2], learn multiscale representations of ECG and sEMG through adaptive wavelet selection, soft gating, cross-scale feature aggregation, and frequency-guided masked pre-training. Nevertheless, three design choices in PhysioWave limit how far this paradigm scales. Its tokenizer expanded every wavelet scale into separate token row, and each encoder was constrained to single fixed input configuration. Both limitations are most severe for EEG, whose clinical montages vary widely across datasets and whose dense electrode arrays rapidly multiply the token count. PhysioWaves multimodal experiments relied on an external pre-trained backbone and combined modalities using fixed learned weights that could not adapt to the signal quality of individual samples. These bottlenecks raise three central questions that anchor this work: how to retain multiscale time-frequency information without multiplying tokens, how to share single architecture across heterogeneous acquisition setups, and how to fuse modalities whose reliability varies across recordings. PhysioWave-T addresses the first two questions by decoupling acquisition-specific processing from representation learning. Each acquisition route, defined by channel count and sampling rate, receives dedicated wavelet front end and sampling-rate-specific patch projection, while sharing single Transformer backbone and name-based channel vocabulary across the modality. Within each front end, dynamic scale folding recombines wavelet subbands prior to tokenization using weights predicted from local IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON PATTERN ANALYSIS AND MACHINE INTELLIGENCE 2 subband statistics and refined by learned synthesis filters. Consequently, the backbone processes CS rather than (J+1)CS tokens regardless of decomposition depth: deeper analysis enriches individual tokens instead of multiplying sequence length. Because folding contains no channel-specific parameters, it transfers unchanged across montages; an unseen downstream configuration requires only attaching lightweight front end to the frozen or fine-tuned backbone and appending any new sensor names to the vocabulary. These mechanisms allow PhysioWave to scale to EEG, yielding unified EEG foundation model as central contribution of this work. Without coercing recordings into common montage, we pre-train 30M-parameter encoder on over 15 four-second windows spanning clinical, research, braincomputer interface, and high-density corpora (19128 channels at 256 and 512 Hz). Across four EEG routes, scale folding reduces Transformer latency by 4.07.2 and peak memory by 6.812.7 over scale expansion, cutting perbatch memory on 128-channel recordings from 32 GB to 2.5 GB. Against BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, and EEGPT, our encoder leads on eight of nine metrics across sleep staging, P300, and error-related negativity detectionincluding on Sleep-EDFx, whose 100 Hz derivations are unseen during pre-training. On two-channel behind-the-ear seizure detection, it reaches 61.4 % sensitivity at 11 false alarms per hour, outperforming LUNA-L with 25.4 versus 40.4 parameters. Pre-training also boosts label efficiency: using just 10 % of KaggleERN labels, the encoder surpasses fully supervised scratch model. Finally, the learned representations capture intrinsic physiology: channel embeddings recover scalp topography without coordinate supervision, and the slowest wavelet scales weight progressively increases from wakefulness to deep sleep. For the third question, reliability-aware latent fusion (RALF) combines this EEG encoder with independently pretrained ECG and sEMG encoders, without joint multimodal pre-training. Each encoder contributes four summary tokens. per-sample reliability score gates that modalitys contribution to attention and the residual unimodal prediction, and missing modalities are masked explicitly. On SeizeIT2, with simultaneous wearable EEG, ECG, and EMG, RALF raises event sensitivity at 11 false alarms per hour from 61.4 % to 78.9 % and window-level AUPRC from 0.321 to 0.399 relative to the best EEG model. All six training variants exceed weighted-logit and concatenation fusion in AUPRC, most clearly on ECG-containing combinations. RALF also retains an AUPRC of at least 0.33 under every tested single-modality corruption. Relative to PhysioWave, the contributions are: Token-efficient multiscale modeling. Dynamic scale folding shortens the sequence by factor of J+1 while retaining adaptive wavelet analysis. We quantify its effects on accuracy, latency, memory, and computation. An EEG foundation model across acquisition configurations. Route-specific front ends and extensible channel vocabularies let one shared 30M-parameter backbone learn from heterogeneous montages and transfer to unseen ones, including two-channel wearable EEG. Reliability-aware multimodal prediction. RALF fuses compact modality summaries using sample-specific reliability estimates. We evaluate it on seizure detection under complete, missing, and corrupted inputs.

sections.title:
2 RELATED WORK
2.1 Physiological Foundation Models
sections.content: Following BERT [3] and MAE [4], masked reconstruction and predictive learning have produced transferable EEG representations. BENDR [5] and Brant [6] established contrastive and predictive pre-training. BIOT tokenizes channel-wise spectral patches [7], LaBraM predicts discrete neural codes [8], EEGPT combines masked reconstruction with spatiotemporal alignment [9], and CBraMod separates spatial and temporal interactions through criss-cross attention [10]. Beyond EEG, ST-MEM [11], HuBERT-ECG [12], and ECG-FM [13] apply masked modeling or self-distillation to ECG, and large wristband datasets support sEMG models for movement and interaction [14], [15]. Generic time-series models such as MOMENT [16] and UniTS [17] pursue broader transfer. These models differ mainly in their tokenization and pre-training targets. PhysioWave-T instead addresses the interface between acquisition and representation: configuration-specific processing precedes shared token space, and multiscale analysis does not lengthen the backbone sequence. 2.2 Multiscale Representations and Heterogeneous Inputs Wavelets localize signal structure in time and frequency [18], [19]. Best-basis selection [20] and coefficient shrinkage [21] adapt this representation to signal structure or noise, and neural wavelet operators make its filters trainable [22]. WaveFormer [1] introduced soft wavelet selection for sEMG, and PhysioWave [2] paired learnable wavelet analysis with frequency-guided pre-training for ECG and sEMG. However, PhysioWave allocated separate token row to every band. PhysioWave-T retains these analysis components but folds the subbands before tokenization, so decomposition depth no longer lengthens the sequence. Generalizing classical bestbasis selection, the fold replaces discrete wavelet-packet tree search with learned, continuous scale mixture. Heterogeneous acquisition poses separate challenge. Perceiver architectures compress variable inputs into latent arrays [23], mixture-of-experts models route tokens among specialized subnetworks [24], [25], and channel-independent designs process each channel separately [26]. In EEG, namebased embeddings identify electrodes [8], [9], graph models encode spatial adjacency [27], and LUNA [28] maps variable electrode sets to fixed set of latent queries. PhysioWave-T selects front end deterministically from acquisition metadata rather than learning token-level routing. It also extends name-based identity to ECG leads and sEMG electrode sites, adding vocabulary entries during downstream adaptation. 2.3 Multimodal Physiological Fusion Combining biosignals improves prediction when modalities carry complementary information, yet acquisition failures rarely affect all sensors equally. Even available modalities may differ substantially in their signal quality. Latent and bottleneck fusion restrict cross-modal interaction to compact summaries [23], [29], avoiding attention over every unimodal token. RALF follows this design and adds sample-specific reliability estimate for each modality, supervised by corruption severity, while explicit masks handle absent inputs. 4 PRE-TRAINING, ADAPTATION, AND MULTIMODAL
FUSION
The EEG, ECG, and sEMG encoders share one pre-training
objective but are trained independently, each on the corpora
of its own modality. A pre-trained encoder can then be
adapted to a downstream configuration or combined with
the other two through reliability-aware latent fusion.
sections.content: 4.1 Self-Supervised Pre-training Pre-training extends PhysioWaves masked reconstruction in two ways: masking acts on the raw input, and the encoder reconstructs two complementary targets (Fig. 1(c) (d)). Masking tokens alone would not suffice for this front end, because convolution and cross-scale fusion mix neighboring samples before tokenization, leaving hidden content accessible through adjacent features. Each window is therefore processed in two views. The clean view supplies reconstruction targets and mask-selection scores, while the online view zeros the selected raw-signal patches before the front end, so their samples never enter the online features. After tokenization, the masked positions are replaced by learned mask token. Patch selection follows PhysioWaves frequency-guided strategy: spectral importance is computed from the summed magnitude spectrum along the clean-view token sequence and combined with uniform noise as = 0.6 + 0.4 z. The highest-scoring 70 % of valid tokens are masked, so spectrally dominant patches are hidden most often and must be inferred from context. For ECG, the six limb leads within temporal patch are masked together, since their linear dependencies would otherwise leak the hidden content, and precordial leads are masked individually. Unavailable channel slots are excluded from both mask selection and reconstruction scoring. Two shallow decoders per sampling rate then predict the masked patches in two spaces. The spectral target is the IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON PATTERN ANALYSIS AND MACHINE INTELLIGENCE 6 with median NMSE and mask 70 % of its patches before the front end. Masked-patch correlations range from 0.79 to 0.89 for the raw-EEG head and from 0.75 to 0.88 for the folded-wavelet head, with one shared backbone serving all four route-specific front ends. Single-channel traces from the same windows  (Fig. 5)  show that predictions recover waveform structure across masked spans of up to three consecutive seconds, reaching correlations of 0.93 and 0.96 on the selected M3CV and HBN channels. The TUEG channel is harder (r = 0.52), although its window-level correlation is 0.79, indicating that reconstruction difficulty varies across channels within one recording. Each corpus is assigned to compatible acquisition route rather than forced into single modality-wide layout. To prevent large datasets from dominating pre-training, corpora are sampled with probability (d) n0.5 for corpus of nd windows, while per-device batch sizes scale inversely with the route token count. During preprocessing, recordings are standardized to common physical units and, where necessary, resampled to the target route rate via anti-aliased polyphase filtering. Channels are then mapped to their named slots and each window is normalized, without applying any additional band-pass filtering. 4.2 Downstream Adaptation downstream task specifies its channel count, sampling rate, and sensor names. The Transformer, channel embedding table, projection, and identity gate are always transferred from the modality checkpoint. Front ends and patch embeddings are transferred when the configuration matches pretraining route, as for PTB-XL on the 12-lead ECG route, and are newly initialized otherwise. Mean-pooled tokens feed two-layer prediction head, and we evaluate three adaptation modes. Fine-tune optimizes all parameters with layer-wise learning-rate decay in the Transformer. Probe freezes transferred components and trains only the head and any newly introduced front-end or adapter parameters. Scratch trains the same architecture from random initialization, isolating the contribution of pre-training under each task protocol. 4.3 Reliability-Aware Multimodal Fusion PhysioWave combines unimodal logits with one learned weight per modality. These weights are fixed after training, so they cannot reflect the degradation of particular sensor in particular window. Scale folding. Scale expansion feeds all J+1 bands to the backbone as separate token rows, giving the Transformer direct access to every subband at four times the sequence length. The dynamic fold scores 0.3 points higher on average with quarter of the tokens, so compressing the scales before tokenization loses nothing that the backbone could have recovered from the longer sequence. How the scales are combined does matter, however. static uniform fold drops the average by 1.6 points and falls 1.3 points below scale expansion, so plain average of the subbands discards information that the expanded representation preserves. Of the 1.6-point gap between the uniform and dynamic folds, the learned synthesis filters account for 0.7 points, since replacing every gs with delta costs that much, and the data-dependent weights α account for the remaining 0.9. Both components are therefore needed to match and then exceed scale expansion, and the full fold achieves this with predictor shared across channels. Fig. 8 quantifies the cost side on one A100 in bf16 with matched route-specific batch sizes. Across the four EEG routes, folding reduces Transformer latency by 4.0 7.2, peak memory by 6.812.7, and FLOPs by 4.35.5. Memory shrinks more than FLOPs because the attention Fig. 8. All three savings grow with token count and peak on the 128-channel route, where batch needs about 32 GB without folding and 2.5 GB with it in this profiling setup. These figures use matched batch sizes and therefore differ from the pre-training memory reported in Section 5.1. The fold itself, including its subband statistics and weighting network, accounts for only 1.52.6 % of the forward pass, so its accuracy benefit comes at negligible cost. Pre-training and adaptation. Removing pre-training lowers the four-metric average by 3.7 points, with the loss concentrated on KaggleERN, where balanced accuracy and AUROC fall by 4.7 and 6.3 points. The adaptation ladder shows why the two tasks differ. On PhysioNet-P300, the frozen encoder is within one balanced-accuracy point of full fine-tuning, and tuning the top two or four blocks changes little, so the pre-trained representation already separates target from non-target responses. On KaggleERN, the frozen encoder reaches only 53.7 %, below the 57.0 % of the scratch model, and balanced accuracy climbs monotonically with the number of tuned blocks: 57.9 % with two, 59.8 % with four, and 61.7 % with the full backbone. Error-related negativity is brief, low-amplitude deflection embedded in ongoing frontocentral activity, and pre-training on four-second windows of clinical EEG does not isolate it on its own. The pre-trained weights nonetheless provide the better starting point, since fine-tuning from them ends 4.7 points above training from scratch. Channel identity. Setting the channel-encoding gate to zero in (12) lowers the average score by 1.8 points, and shuffling channel names lowers it by 2.1. The second number is the more informative one: the shuffled model keeps the same embedding parameters and receives spatial information that is simply wrong, and it performs worse than model given no spatial information at all. The benefit of correct identity therefore comes from the scalp geometry the embeddings encode (Section 6.1), not from added capacity. The losses concentrate on PhysioNet-P300, where removing channel encoding costs 2.6 balanced-accuracy and 2.8 AUROC points, compared with 0.9 and 1.1 on KaggleERN. The P300 response has well-defined parietal distribution, so knowing which electrode produced each token helps locate it; the errorrelated negativity is spatially more diffuse, and the task relies less on electrode identity. Both alternatives add trainable readout capacity on top of the backbone, and both hurt. Under full fine-tuning, the backbone can already arrange its tokens so that simple average is linearly separable, and the extra readout parameters mainly add variance on datasets of this size. The temporal head, designed for probing frozen encoder in EEGPT, is the more complex of the two and suffers most. Label efficiency. Reducing supervision to 10 % of the labels costs the pre-trained encoder 4.8 points on average, against 8.7 points for the matched scratch model, so pretraining roughly halves the loss from scarce labels. The absolute numbers on KaggleERN are more telling: with 10 % of the labels, the pre-trained encoder already exceeds the scratch model trained on all labels, by 0.8 balanced-accuracy and 1.2 AUROC points, and with 25 % the margins widen to 2.6 and 3.8 points. One tenth of the annotations is therefore enough to match full-data training from scratch on this task. The effect is weaker on PhysioNet-P300, where the scratch model is itself strong; there, 25 % of the labels bring the pre-trained encoder within 0.9 balanced-accuracy points of full-data scratch. Missing electrodes. Dropping 25 % and 50 % of the electrodes at test time, without imputation or retraining, lowers the average score by 2.1 and 4.2 points, so performance degrades gradually and in proportion to the electrodes removed. With quarter of the electrodes missing, KaggleERN balanced accuracy remains 60.4 %, still above EEGPT with the full montage (58.4 %), and with half missing it nearly matches that baseline at 58.3 % and still exceeds the scratch model with every electrode (57.0 %). Because absent slots are masked and the remaining channels keep their name embeddings, the encoder continues to interpret the electrodes it receives without any adaptation to the reduced montage.

We examine the trained encoders through their spectral

We test whether these embeddings nevertheless encode scalp geometry by relating their pairwise cosine similarities to geodesic electrode distances (Fig. 9a). For the 130 electrodes of the 10-5 system and the 128 EGI HydroCel positions, the Spearman correlations are ρ = 0.19 and 0.25, more than twelve standard deviations from the permutation-null mean (p < 0.001 over 2,000 draws), whereas the untrained table shows no association (ρ = 0.01). The structure is even clearer locally. The five nearest neighbors of each electrode in embedding space lie at mean angular distance of 56 on the scalp for 10-5 names and 44 for EGI, compared with 8488 after name shuffling, and the electrode-centered maps for Fz, Cz, Pz, Oz, T7, and T8 (Fig. 9b) show similarity concentrated around each reference site. Because volume conduction makes neighboring electrodes record overlapping mixtures of the same sources, pre-training on raw signals is enough for the vocabulary to recover scalp topology from names alone. This learned geometry also explains the ablation result in Section 5.6, where shuffling channel names costs more than removing channel encoding entirely. 6.2 Modality-Specific Spectral Adaptation All front ends start from the same uniformly mixed filter bank, so any difference after pre-training is learned from the signals themselves (Fig. 10a). The sEMG front ends also widen their low-pass branch, with 3 dB cutoffs rising from 125 Hz at initialization to 356418 Hz. sections.title:
7 DISCUSSION
PhysioWave-T rests on one organizing principle: everything
that depends on how a signal was acquired is handled
before tokenization, and everything that depends on what it
contains is learned afterward by a shared backbone. This is
why a single 30 M-parameter EEG encoder can learn from 19-
to 128-channel montages and then transfer to a two-channel
wearable, and why decomposition depth becomes a choice
about the content of each token instead of the length of
the sequence. The analyses show that the efficiency costs
nothing in physiological meaning: identically initialized
front ends settle on the QRS, 100–200 Hz, and γ ranges
for their modalities, the folding weights track sleep stages
without stage labels, and the channel vocabulary recovers
scalp topology from electrode names alone, which makes
coordinates an unnecessary input and lets the same identity
mechanism cover ECG leads and sEMG sites.
sections.content: The experiments also clarify when pre-training matters and how to use it. Its benefit is smallest where downstream data already cover the test conditions and largest under distribution shift and label scarcity, as in inter-session sEMG and KaggleERN, where tenth of the labels match fulldata training from scratch. Some tasks are served by the frozen representation, whereas subtle responses such as error-related negativity require adapting the backbone, so probing first and fine-tuning when needed is the natural recipe. For multimodal monitoring, RALF shows that persample reliability pays off when artifact-prone ECG must be weighed against EEG and at strict false-alarm budgets, and its scores fall in proportion to how much signal corruption leaves. The corruptions studied here are synthetic; prospective recordings with natural sensor failures, joint multimodal pre-training, and new routes for modalities such as photoplethysmography are the next steps.

8 CONCLUSION
PhysioWave-T shows that a biosignal foundation model
can accommodate heterogeneous acquisition without paying
for it in sequence length. Route-specific wavelet front ends
and name-based channel embeddings let one backbone per
modality learn from any sensor configuration, dynamic scale
folding keeps multiscale analysis within C S tokens, and the
resulting EEG, ECG, and sEMG encoders lead the compared
models across sleep staging, event-related potentials, cardiac
diagnosis, and gesture recognition while cutting Transformer
memory by up to an order of magnitude. Reliability-aware
fusion extends them to multimodal seizure detection under
missing and corrupted inputs, and new acquisition setups
attach to the released backbones with a new front end instead
of a new model.

Basis selection becomes more decisive with depth (Fig. 10b). At level one, every route keeps mixture over its five candidate wavelets, whereas at level three the weights concentrate on single basis within each modalitys bank. Fine resolutions contain heterogeneous transients that benefit from blend of wavelet shapes, while the smoother coarse approximations are described well by one basis, and the selector learns this division without supervision. 6.3 Scale Allocation Across Sleep Stages Sleep staging offers direct test of whether the folding weights track physiology, since sleep stages are defined largely by their dominant rhythms. We analyze the encoder fine-tuned on Sleep-EDFx over 37,902 thirty-second windows from 14 test subjects, grouping the weights by expertannotated stage (Fig. 11a). The folding network receives only signal-derived subband statistics and is never told the stage, yet the weight of the slowest scale, a3 (below 6.25 Hz), rises steadily from wake to N3 and returns toward its wake value in REM. This trajectory mirrors the electrophysiology of sleep: slow-wave activity dominates N3, whereas REM EEG resembles the low-amplitude, mixed-frequency activity of wake. Within subjects (Fig. 11b), the wake-to-N3 increase holds in all 13 subjects with both stages on Pz-Oz (Wilcoxon = 2.4 104) and in 10 of 13 on Fpz-Cz (p = 0.048), so the effect is consistent across individuals. The two derivations nonetheless receive different scale mixtures from the same shared network. At the window level (Fig. 11c), the slowest-scale weight correlates positively with δ-band power share on Pz-Oz (ρ = 0.21) but negatively on Fpz-Cz (ρ = 0.22). Fpz-Cz also records ocular activity, whose low-frequency power rises with eye movements during wake and REM, so δ-band power on this derivation is not clean marker of slow-wave sleep. The fold follows the sleep stage on both derivations while responding differently to their raw low-frequency power, showing that it allocates scales according to what the low-frequency content represents on each derivation.
